name: Emeka Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's my wife Grace's family farm, about eighty hectares: some sheep, a few beef cattle, a hundred laying hens, potatoes and vegetables, and a farm shop at the gate where we sell all of it. I'm up at six for the animals with my father-in-law Arthur, then I open the shop at nine and stand behind the counter until one. Afternoons I'm in the field, or cutting meat with the butcher who comes on Thursdays, or fixing whatever Arthur says I broke.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years in the army, I left as a sergeant. When Arthur turned seventy, Grace said the farm needed a man who could follow orders and lift things, so here I am. I'm good at early mornings and keeping the shop in order, but I'm still learning the farming, and Arthur reminds me of that daily.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The shop. People come in on Saturday morning and they know my name and I know theirs, and Mrs Patel tells me about her grandson every week whether I ask or not. That's a community. Before church on Sunday I count the honesty box for the eggs, and it's always right, nearly to the coin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the clever people have their clever tools, it's nothing to do with us. People will still want eggs from a hen they can see from the car park. I wouldn't say it online, I'm not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm glad. I don't use any of it and I don't intend to. We keep the shop accounts in a book and the till is a till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I'd planned. Extend the shop into the old dairy, about twenty thousand, so we can have a proper cold counter for meat. I'd pay for it from savings, not a loan, because my army pension covers our family costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the honesty box is always right. What does that tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That most people are decent when you trust them. That's what this valley is like, and I'd guard it. You don't need a computer for trust, you need a box and a sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your son Chidi, is he interested in the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fourteen and more interested in football, but he does the hens before school without being asked twice. I'd like him to learn a trade, a real one with an apprenticeship. Grace wants him to go to university, so we have that discussion every Christmas.

S0.say: I'd say let the clever people have their clever tools, it's nothing to do with us. People will still want eggs from a hen they can see from the car park.
S0.think: Privately I'm glad it stays small. I don't use any of it and don't intend to; the shop accounts are in a book and the till is a till.
S0.do: Extends the farm shop into the old dairy for about twenty thousand, paid from savings rather than a loan. Keeps the accounts on paper.
S0.quote: You don't need a computer for trust, you need a box and a sign.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka speaks with the order and directness of his army years. His world is the shop counter, the honesty box and church, and he guards that sense of trust. His army pension gives him a strong floor, and he mentions it without any fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if companies stop training young people, that's a scandal, and they should be ashamed. The army trained me from nothing at seventeen, and that's how it should work. Firms should take on apprentices, not wait for the government to pay them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a beginner myself, at forty-three, being trained by a man of seventy-four. If Arthur weren't family, I'd never have got this chance. So I worry for the young ones who have no Arthur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer a Saturday job in the shop to a youngster from church, a proper one with a wage and some responsibility. And I'd ask Arthur to teach me lambing properly this spring, instead of just watching him. I wouldn't change anything with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little worried for the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you give the Saturday job to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a girl called Abigail, sixteen, who helps with the church tea after the service and never drops a cup. She'd do the till and the eggs and talk to customers. Responsibility early makes people, I believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms shouldn't wait for the government. Should government do anything at all here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make it easier for small businesses to take on apprentices, with less paperwork. That's all. I don't want handouts, I want them to get out of the way.

S1.say: I'd say it's a scandal if companies stop training young people. The army trained me from nothing at seventeen, and firms should take on apprentices themselves, not wait for government money.
S1.think: Privately I'm a beginner too, at forty-three, learning from a man of seventy-four. If Arthur weren't family I'd never have had this chance, so I worry for the young ones with no Arthur.
S1.do: Offers sixteen-year-old Abigail from church a paid Saturday job in the shop with real responsibility. Asks Arthur to teach him lambing properly in spring and changes nothing to do with computers.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry for young people.
S1.quote: So I worry for the young ones who have no Arthur.
S1.fieldNote: His traditional views come out as a strong belief in employers training people, not in state support. He is very aware that family gave him his chance. His answer is to give someone from church a first job, which fits his idea of community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people in offices will need to roll up their sleeves and find new work, and families and churches should help them do it. I wouldn't want the government throwing money around. I'd say that at the church lunch and some people would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know some of my customers would be hurt. The farm shop does well because town people with office jobs drive out on Saturday and pay a bit more for our sausages. If they're laid off, they go to the supermarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on extending the shop until I see how Saturday takings go for three months. I'd make sure we have cheaper things on the counter, like eggs, potatoes, soup bones, so people can still come. And I'd tell our church group to keep an eye on families in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, but for the shop and the people who come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a regular customer lost their job, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give them a discount and not tell anyone. There's a man called Mr Hughes who comes every week for a pork pie. If he lost his job, his pork pie would cost a bit less, and that would be between him and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction between not wanting government help and wanting the church to step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. The church knows the family's name, the government knows a number. I'd rather people were helped by people.

S2.say: I'd say office workers will need to roll up their sleeves and find new work, with families and churches helping. I wouldn't want the government throwing money around.
S2.think: Privately I know the shop does well because office workers from town pay a bit more for our sausages on Saturdays. If they're laid off, they'll go to the supermarket.
S2.do: Holds off on the shop extension until he sees three months of Saturday takings. Puts cheaper items like eggs, potatoes and soup bones on the counter and asks the church group to watch for families in trouble.
S2.feel: Uneasy for the shop and its customers rather than himself.
S2.quote: If he lost his job, his pork pie would cost a bit less, and that would be between him and me.
S2.fieldNote: His views on help are consistent: people helping people, not the state. The quiet discount for Mr Hughes shows how he lives that out. He has a sharp sense of how his shop depends on town office workers' spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should stay with the people who earned them, but those people have a duty to their communities. I don't trust politicians to share it out fairly, they'll fight over it and waste it. I'd say pray, work, and look after your neighbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't like this one. A political crisis means disorder, and I've seen what disorder looks like in other countries, on deployment. If the country is angry and divided, a farm shop on a quiet road isn't as safe as it feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep more cash at hand and less in the bank, maybe two months' worth, just in case. I'd make sure the farm can feed us and the neighbours for a while, which it can. And I'd go to the parish council meetings, which I've been avoiding, because in a crisis local people need to be organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit watchful, like the old days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you see on deployment that comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Towns where the shops closed because nobody trusted the money any more. People bartering bread. I'm not saying that happens here, but I've seen how quickly ordinary life can turn when people stop believing in fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your land would be worth a lot more in this picture. Would you think about selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's Grace's family land, and one day Chidi's or Ruth's. You don't sell your inheritance because someone in the city has money to burn.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should stay with those who earned them, but they have a duty to their communities. I don't trust politicians to share it fairly; pray, work and look after your neighbour.
S3.think: Privately I don't like this one, because a political crisis means disorder, and I've seen disorder on deployment. If the country is angry and divided, a farm shop on a quiet road isn't as safe as it feels.
S3.do: Keeps about two months of cash at home and checks the farm could feed his family and neighbours. Starts attending parish council meetings he has been avoiding.
S3.feel: Uneasy and watchful, like his army days.
S3.quote: I've seen how quickly ordinary life can turn when people stop believing in fairness.
S3.fieldNote: The army past shapes this scenario more than any other: he thinks of order, supplies and local organising. He is firmly against selling the family land, framed as inheritance rather than money. His trust goes to neighbours and church, not politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are a mistake and the country will regret it. Farming is how a nation feeds itself and how young people learn to work. I'd say it to anyone who asked, and plenty who didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this frightens me more than I'd show. The big farms will buy robots and sell meat and vegetables cheaper than I can, and my shop survives on people choosing us anyway. And if robots do the hard work, what does a man like me, who's good at hard work, do with his days?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy any robots, I know that. I'd make the shop about people: Saturday breakfasts, the butcher cutting meat in front of customers, school visits to see the lambs. And I'd talk to the national farmers' group about pushing for clear labels, so people can see what was grown by hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly, and a bit angry. I don't like feeling useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You believe in free markets, but here you'd want something to slow the robots down. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You've caught me there, and I'll admit it. I believe in markets, but a market that destroys families and communities isn't a market I want. Maybe I'd settle for honest labels and let people choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth, your daughter, if she asked whether the farm will be there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the farm will be there as long as we are, and that we'll pray about the rest. Ruth is ten and she believes everything I tell her, so I'd have to mean it. I'd mean it.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms are a mistake the country will regret, because farming is how a nation feeds itself and how young people learn to work. I'd say it to anyone, asked or not.
S4.think: Privately this frightens me more than I'd show, because big robot farms will sell cheaper than my shop can. And if robots do the hard work, I wonder what a man who's good at hard work does with his days.
S4.do: Refuses to buy robots and turns the shop into more of a people place, with Saturday breakfasts, live butchery and school visits to the lambs. Pushes through a national farmers' group for clear labels showing food grown by hands.
S4.feel: Frightened and a little angry, with a sharp dislike of feeling useless.
S4.quote: And if robots do the hard work, what does a man like me, who's good at hard work, do with his days?
S4.fieldNote: When I named the gap between his free-market views and his wish to slow robots down, he admitted it straight away and settled on labels. His fear is about dignity and purpose as much as money. Faith is his last word when he thinks about his daughter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, the last one. The others hurt other people more than me, but that one hurts my purpose. What would help is honest labels so customers can choose food grown by people, and support for apprenticeships so young ones still learn farming with their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. I'd say that whatever happens with all this, the people who come through the shop door on Saturday still need somewhere to belong. That's what I'm really selling, not sausages.

headlineQuote: The people who come through the shop door on Saturday still need somewhere to belong. That's what I'm really selling, not sausages.
portrait: Emeka Silva spent twenty-two years in the army before joining his wife's family farm, where he runs the farm shop and learns the farming from his seventy-four-year-old father-in-law. He is orderly, plain-spoken and devout, never uses AI, and keeps the accounts in a book. He believes in work, apprenticeships and church support rather than government help, and he lives it out with quiet discounts for struggling customers. The office scenarios worry him for his shop's town customers, the political crisis stirs memories of disorder on deployment, and the robot picture frightens him most because it threatens his sense of purpose.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because it threatens his sense of purpose and his shop's ability to compete with big robot-run farms.
whatWouldHelp: Honest labels so customers can choose food grown by people, and support for apprenticeships so young people can still learn farming by hand.
